content: 1. The certification of competency scheme has led to the regular training of staff, enhanced knowledge among employees, and increased attention by workers to their methods. 2. The Water Sector Regulatory Council in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, oversees a wide range of regulatory functions such as licensing, operational monitoring, handling complaints, setting tariffs, and implementing incentive-based regulations. 3. The Council regulates over 300 water and sanitation service providers, including small-scale water suppliers, which consist of municipalities, village councils, water associations, NGOs, private water companies, and regional utilities. 4. Material safety standards have been introduced to govern the composition of products and materials that come into contact with drinking water, aligning with international and neighboring countries' standards to facilitate material imports. 5. These standards cover critical components of water supply systems, such as materials used in pumps, pipelines, and filling stations. 6. Recognizing the challenges faced by water suppliers in meeting these standards, the Council supports a phased implementation approach, monitors compliance, and advises on corrective actions in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, central water authority, and local authorities. 7. This collaborative approach has effectively encouraged water suppliers to progressively upgrade their systems to meet the standards, supported by incentive-based regulations and performance benchmarking. 8. In Ghana, research in 2017 revealed that 6% of rural water supplies had lead levels exceeding the national limit of 10 µg/L, with leaded brass components identified as the primary source of contamination. 9. Despite existing material safety standards, compliance has been limited due to inadequate quality control and assurance systems, leading to false claims by manufacturers about lead-free products. 10. Regulatory initiatives in Ghana include verifying the quality of imported materials, certifying materials for water supply construction, and enhancing oversight of water supply activities. 11. X-ray fluorescence spectrometry is being used to test water supply components for compliance, while awareness and capacity-building efforts are being directed at local stakeholders to improve material testing. 12. In Wales, private water supplies, defined as those not connected to public mains, have been subject to risk assessments since 2010, leading to significant improvements in microbial water quality. 13. The percentage of water samples with Escherichia coli contamination dropped from over 20% in 2010 to less than 7% in 2022, attributed to proactive risk management. 14. In the Asia-Pacific region, a study of 99 water supplies across 12 countries between 2014 and 2016 showed statistically significant improvements in operations and management practices, including monitoring, emergency response plans, and consumer education. 15. In Germany, the revised EU Drinking Water Directive mandates risk assessment and management for water suppliers serving at least 500 people or providing 100 m³ per day, with additional requirements for smaller suppliers. 16. Operators of all water supplies, excluding individual households, must inspect catchment and abstraction areas annually to manage risks to drinking water quality. 17. In the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, rural water suppliers were given 10 years to comply with water safety plan requirements introduced in 2014, allowing health authorities time to provide training and support. 18. In Madagascar, Tatirano Social Enterprise collaborates with the Ministry of Water to implement the national Water Code, focusing on proactive inspection and maintenance of water supplies in remote areas to ensure microbial and chemical safety. 19. Field agents, primarily local women, are trained to inspect water supplies daily, with results displayed online for transparency and accountability. 20. In Bhutan, water safety plans have been required since 2016, with templates tailored to the capacities of municipal and community-managed supplies. 21. Municipal supplies use electronic templates with detailed documentation, while community supplies use simpler, paper-based templates completed during workshops. 22. In Finland, water safety plan implementation is mandatory for all drinking water suppliers, with requirements varying by supply size. 23. Comprehensive web-based tools developed by the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health facilitate water safety plan development and serve as training platforms.
